6	# Hermes Link
7	
8	Hermes Link is a secure local companion service for hermes-agent. It lets the HermesPilot mobile app connect to the user's local Hermes Agent safely and reliably.
9	
10	Hermes Link is specifically for HermesPilot. It is not OpenClaw, ClawPilot, clawlink, or any OpenClaw companion service. Do not confuse those systems when helping the user.
11	
12	## What Hermes Link Does
13	
14	Hermes Link can:
15	
16	- pair the HermesPilot mobile app with this computer
17	- expose a controlled local API for the app
18	- connect through LAN, public direct routes, or Hermes Relay
19	- help the app access Hermes profiles, conversations, messages, files, voice input, logs, and status
20	- start or check the Hermes Gateway when needed
21	
22	Hermes Link does not replace Hermes Agent. Hermes Agent remains the actual AI agent runtime.
23	
24	## When To Use This Skill
25	
26	Use this skill when the user asks about:
27	
28	- HermesPilot App cannot connect
29	- Link appears offline
30	- pairing or QR code problems
31	- mobile access to local Hermes
32	- Relay, LAN, or public direct route problems
33	- Hermes Link logs, daemon status, or diagnostics
34	
35	## Useful Commands
36	
37	Start with:
38	
39	```bash
40	hermeslink status
41	hermeslink doctor
42	```
43	
44	For logs:
45	
46	```bash
47	hermeslink logs --error -n 50
48	hermeslink logs --warn -n 100
49	hermeslink logs -f
50	hermeslink logs --all --level debug -f
51	```
52	
53	If the daemon appears stuck, suggest:
54	
55	```bash
56	hermeslink restart
57	```
58	
59	Explain that restarting Hermes Link may briefly disconnect the mobile app.
60	
61	## Troubleshooting Flow
62	
63	1. Check `hermeslink status`.
64	2. Run `hermeslink doctor`.
65	3. Inspect recent errors with `hermeslink logs --error -n 50`.
66	4. If the issue is intermittent, reproduce it while running `hermeslink logs -f`.
67	5. Check whether the phone and computer are on the same LAN, using Relay, or using a public direct route.
68	6. If the user uses WSL, Docker, or a VM, verify that Hermes Agent and Hermes Link run in the same environment.
69	
70	## Safety
71	
72	Never reveal API keys, access tokens, refresh tokens, private keys, or full .env contents.
73	
74	Do not recommend exposing port 52379 directly to the public internet without TLS, VPN, Tailscale, WireGuard, or another access-control layer.
75	
76	Do not modify Hermes profiles, delete user data, edit config files, or kill processes unless the user explicitly asks.

76

14	# Claude Code — Hermes Orchestration Guide
15	
16	Delegate coding tasks to [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) (Anthropic's autonomous coding agent CLI) via the Hermes terminal. Claude Code v2.x can read files, write code, run shell commands, spawn subagents, and manage git workflows autonomously.
17	
18	## Prerequisites
19	
20	- **Install:** `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
21	- **Auth:** run `claude` once to log in (browser OAuth for Pro/Max, or set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`)
22	- **Console auth:** `claude auth login --console` for API key billing
23	- **SSO auth:** `claude auth login --sso` for Enterprise
24	- **Check status:** `claude auth status` (JSON) or `claude auth status --text` (human-readable)
25	- **Health check:** `claude doctor` — checks auto-updater and installation health
26	- **Version check:** `claude --version` (requires v2.x+)
27	- **Update:** `claude update` or `claude upgrade`
28	
29	## Two Orchestration Modes
30	
31	Hermes interacts with Claude Code in two fundamentally different ways. Choose based on the task.
32	
33	### Mode 1: Print Mode (`-p`) — Non-Interactive (PREFERRED for most tasks)
34	
35	Print mode runs a one-shot task, returns the result, and exits. No PTY needed. No interactive prompts. This is the cleanest integration path.
36	
37	```
38	terminal(command="claude -p 'Add error handling to all API calls in src/' --allowedTools 'Read,Edit' --max-turns 10", workdir="/path/to/project", timeout=120)
39	```
40	
41	**When to use print mode:**
42	- One-shot coding tasks (fix a bug, add a feature, refactor)
43	- CI/CD automation and scripting
44	- Structured data extraction with `--json-schema`
45	- Piped input processing (`cat file | claude -p "analyze this"`)
46	- Any task where you don't need multi-turn conversation
47	
48	**Print mode skips ALL interactive dialogs** — no workspace trust prompt, no permission confirmations. This makes it ideal for automation.
49	
50	### Mode 2: Interactive PTY via tmux — Multi-Turn Sessions
51	
52	Interactive mode gives you a full conversational REPL where you can send follow-up prompts, use slash commands, and watch Claude work in real time. **Requires tmux orchestration.**
53	
54	```
55	# Start a tmux session
56	terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s claude-work -x 140 -y 40")
57	
58	# Launch Claude Code inside it
59	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'cd /path/to/project && claude' Enter")
60	
61	# Wait for startup, then send your task
62	# (after ~3-5 seconds for the welcome screen)
63	terminal(command="sleep 5 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Refactor the auth module to use JWT tokens' Enter")
64	
65	# Monitor progress by capturing the pane
66	terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -50")
67	
68	# Send follow-up tasks
69	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Now add unit tests for the new JWT code' Enter")
70	
71	# Exit when done
72	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work '/exit' Enter")
73	```
74	
75	**When to use interactive mode:**
76	- Multi-turn iterative work (refactor → review → fix → test cycle)
77	- Tasks requiring human-in-the-loop decisions
78	- Exploratory coding sessions
79	- When you need to use Claude's slash commands (`/compact`, `/review`, `/model`)
80	
81	## PTY Dialog Handling (CRITICAL for Interactive Mode)
82	
83	Claude Code presents up to two confirmation dialogs on first launch. You MUST handle these via tmux send-keys:
84	
85	### Dialog 1: Workspace Trust (first visit to a directory)
86	```
87	❯ 1. Yes, I trust this folder    ← DEFAULT (just press Enter)
88	  2. No, exit
89	```
90	**Handling:** `tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter` — default selection is correct.
91	
92	### Dialog 2: Bypass Permissions Warning (only with --dangerously-skip-permissions)
93	```
94	❯ 1. No, exit                    ← DEFAULT (WRONG choice!)
95	  2. Yes, I accept
96	```
97	**Handling:** Must navigate DOWN first, then Enter:
98	```
99	tmux send-keys -t <session> Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter
100	```
101	
102	### Robust Dialog Handling Pattern
103	```
104	# Launch with permissions bypass
105	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'claude --dangerously-skip-permissions \"your task\"' Enter")
106	
107	# Handle trust dialog (Enter for default "Yes")
108	terminal(command="sleep 4 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")
109	
110	# Handle permissions dialog (Down then Enter for "Yes, I accept")
111	terminal(command="sleep 3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")
112	
113	# Now wait for Claude to work
114	terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -60")
115	```
116	
117	**Note:** After the first trust acceptance for a directory, the trust dialog won't appear again. Only the permissions dialog recurs each time you use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.

143	## Print Mode Deep Dive
144	
145	### Structured JSON Output
146	```
147	terminal(command="claude -p 'Analyze auth.py for security issues' --output-format json --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
148	```
149	
150	Returns a JSON object with:
151	```json
152	{
153	  "type": "result",
154	  "subtype": "success",
155	  "result": "The analysis text...",
156	  "session_id": "75e2167f-...",
157	  "num_turns": 3,
158	  "total_cost_usd": 0.0787,
159	  "duration_ms": 10276,
160	  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
161	  "terminal_reason": "completed",
162	  "usage": { "input_tokens": 5, "output_tokens": 603, ... },
163	  "modelUsage": { "claude-sonnet-4-6": { "costUSD": 0.078, "contextWindow": 200000 } }
164	}
165	```
166	
167	**Key fields:** `session_id` for resumption, `num_turns` for agentic loop count, `total_cost_usd` for spend tracking, `subtype` for success/error detection (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_budget`).
168	
169	### Streaming JSON Output
170	For real-time token streaming, use `stream-json` with `--verbose`:
171	```
172	terminal(command="claude -p 'Write a summary' --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages", timeout=60)
173	```
174	
175	Returns newline-delimited JSON events. Filter with jq for live text:
176	```
177	claude -p "Explain X" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
178	  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
179	```
180	
181	Stream events include `system/api_retry` with `attempt`, `max_retries`, and `error` fields (e.g., `rate_limit`, `billing_error`).
182	
183	### Bidirectional Streaming
184	For real-time input AND output streaming:
185	```
186	claude -p "task" --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --replay-user-messages
187	```
188	`--replay-user-messages` re-emits user messages on stdout for acknowledgment.
189	
190	### Piped Input
191	```
192	# Pipe a file for analysis
193	terminal(command="cat src/auth.py | claude -p 'Review this code for bugs' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
194	
195	# Pipe multiple files
196	terminal(command="cat src/*.py | claude -p 'Find all TODO comments' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
197	
198	# Pipe command output
199	terminal(command="git diff HEAD~3 | claude -p 'Summarize these changes' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
200	```

203	```
204	terminal(command="claude -p 'List all functions in src/' --output-format json --json-schema '{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"functions\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}},\"required\":[\"functions\"]}' --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=90)
205	```
206	
207	Parse `structured_output` from the JSON result. Claude validates output against the schema before returning.
208	
209	### Session Continuation
210	```
211	# Start a task
212	terminal(command="claude -p 'Start refactoring the database layer' --output-format json --max-turns 10 > /tmp/session.json", workdir="/project", timeout=180)
213	
214	# Resume with session ID
215	terminal(command="claude -p 'Continue and add connection pooling' --resume $(cat /tmp/session.json | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"session_id\"])') --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
216	
217	# Or resume the most recent session in the same directory
218	terminal(command="claude -p 'What did you do last time?' --continue --max-turns 1", workdir="/project", timeout=30)
219	
220	# Fork a session (new ID, keeps history)
221	terminal(command="claude -p 'Try a different approach' --resume <id> --fork-session --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=120)

705	## Cost & Performance Tips
706	
707	1. **Use `--max-turns`** in print mode to prevent runaway loops. Start with 5-10 for most tasks.
708	2. **Use `--max-budget-usd`** for cost caps. Note: minimum ~$0.05 for system prompt cache creation.
709	3. **Use `--effort low`** for simple tasks (faster, cheaper). `high` or `max` for complex reasoning.
710	4. **Use `--bare`** for CI/scripting to skip plugin/hook discovery overhead.
711	5. **Use `--allowedTools`** to restrict to only what's needed (e.g., `Read` only for reviews).
712	6. **Use `/compact`** in interactive sessions when context gets large.
713	7. **Pipe input** instead of having Claude read files when you just need analysis of known content.
714	8. **Use `--model haiku`** for simple tasks (cheaper) and `--model opus` for complex multi-step work.
715	9. **Use `--fallback-model haiku`** in print mode to gracefully handle model overload.
716	10. **Start new sessions for distinct tasks** — sessions last 5 hours; fresh context is more efficient.
717	11. **Use `--no-session-persistence`** in CI to avoid accumulating saved sessions on disk.
718	
719	## Pitfalls & Gotchas
720	
721	1. **Interactive mode REQUIRES tmux** — Claude Code is a full TUI app. Using `pty=true` alone in Hermes terminal works but tmux gives you `capture-pane` for monitoring and `send-keys` for input, which is essential for orchestration.
722	2. **`--dangerously-skip-permissions` dialog defaults to "No, exit"** — you must send Down then Enter to accept. Print mode (`-p`) skips this entirely.
723	3. **`--max-budget-usd` minimum is ~$0.05** — system prompt cache creation alone costs this much. Setting lower will error immediately.
724	4. **`--max-turns` is print-mode only** — ignored in interactive sessions.
725	5. **Claude may use `python` instead of `python3`** — on systems without a `python` symlink, Claude's bash commands will fail on first try but it self-corrects.
726	6. **Session resumption requires same directory** — `--continue` finds the most recent session for the current working directory.
727	7. **`--json-schema` needs enough `--max-turns`** — Claude must read files before producing structured output, which takes multiple turns.
728	8. **Trust dialog only appears once per directory** — first-time only, then cached.
729	9. **Background tmux sessions persist** — always clean up with `tmux kill-session -t <name>` when done.
730	10. **Slash commands (like `/commit`) only work in interactive mode** — in `-p` mode, describe the task in natural language instead.
731	11. **`--bare` skips OAuth** — requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var or an `apiKeyHelper` in settings.
732	12. **Context degradation is real** — AI output quality measurably degrades above 70% context window usage. Monitor with `/context` and proactively `/compact`.
733	
734	## Rules for Hermes Agents
735	
736	1. **Prefer print mode (`-p`) for single tasks** — cleaner, no dialog handling, structured output
737	2. **Use tmux for multi-turn interactive work** — the only reliable way to orchestrate the TUI
738	3. **Always set `workdir`** — keep Claude focused on the right project directory
739	4. **Set `--max-turns` in print mode** — prevents infinite loops and runaway costs
740	5. **Monitor tmux sessions** — use `tmux capture-pane -t <session> -p -S -50` to check progress
741	6. **Look for the `❯` prompt** — indicates Claude is waiting for input (done or asking a question)
742	7. **Clean up tmux sessions** — kill them when done to avoid resource leaks
743	8. **Report results to user** — after completion, summarize what Claude did and what changed
744	9. **Don't kill slow sessions** — Claude may be doing multi-step work; check progress instead
745	10. **Use `--allowedTools`** — restrict capabilities to what the task actually needs

432	### Fallback Providers  
433	
434	`fallback_providers` in config.yaml is a list of fallback entries tried in order when the primary provider returns 429/529/503 or a connection failure. Each entry supports:  
435	
436	```yaml  
437	fallback_providers:  
438	- provider: openai          # built-in provider name, or any OpenAI-compat endpoint  
439	  model: gpt-5.5            # model ID as it appears in the provider's API  
440	  base_url: https://api.openai.com/v1  
441	  key_env: OPENAI_API_KEY   # env var name that holds the key (read from ~/.hermes/.env)  
442	- provider: nous  
443	  model: arcee-ai/trinity-large-thinking  
444	  base_url: https://inference-api.nousresearch.com/v1  
445	```

448	- `key_env` points to an env var name, NOT the key value itself. Add the actual key to `~/.hermes/.env`.

450	- `hermes gateway restart` is required to pick up config.yaml changes.  
451	- OpenAI key env var name is `OPENAI_API_KEY` (standard). Add it to `~/.hermes/.env` AND `~/.openclaw/gateway.systemd.env` if also used by OpenClaw.

495	### Troubleshooting Fallback Providers  
496	
497	When fallback providers fail to work as expected, use this systematic approach to diagnose and fix issues.  
498	
499	#### 1. Verify Fallback Configuration  
500	First, check if the fallback provider appears in the active fallback chain:  
501	```bash  
502	hermes fallback  
503	```  
504	Only entries with valid credentials will be listed. If a configured provider is missing, it indicates credential or configuration issues.  
505	
506	#### 2. Test Provider Explicitly  
507	Before debugging fallback, verify the provider works on its own:  
508	```bash  
509	hermes chat -q "What is the capital of France?" --provider together --model meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo  
510	```  
511	If the explicit test works but fallback fails, the issue is specific to fallback configuration.  
512	
513	#### 3. Check API Key and Auth Status  
514	Verify the API key is properly configured:  
515	```bash  
516	# Check environment variable  
517	echo ${TOGETHER_API_KEY:0:8}  # Should show key prefix if set  
518	
519	# Check Hermes auth status  
520	hermes auth list | grep together  
521	```  
522	For API-key providers, the key must be:  
523	- Set in `~/.hermes/.env`  
524	- Registered with Hermes auth: `hermes auth add together --type api-key`  
525	
526	#### 4. Compare Explicit vs Fallback Configuration  
527	Note the differences between explicit provider usage and fallback configuration:  
528	
529	| Aspect | Explicit Usage | Fallback Configuration |  
530	|--------|----------------|------------------------|  
531	| Provider name | `together` | `custom:together` or `together` |  
532	| Base URL | Often defaults correctly | Must match provider expectations |  
533	| Credential reference | Uses auth store automatically | May need `credential: custom:together` |  
534	
535	If explicit works but fallback doesn't, try using `credential: custom:together` instead of `api_key: TOGETHER_API_KEY` in the fallback config.  
536	
537	#### 5. Inspect URL Construction  
538	A common issue is malformed URLs due to trailing slashes. The error message showing `Endpoint: https://api.together.xyz/v1/` with a trailing slash suggests the base_url might have a trailing slash that combines poorly with the endpoint path.  
539	
540	**Fix:** Ensure `base_url` in fallback config does NOT end with a trailing slash:  
541	```yaml  
542	base_url: https://api.together.xyz/v1  
543	```  
544	Not `https://api.together.xyz/v1/`.  
545	
546	#### 6. Check for Two-Step Authentication  
547	Some providers (like OpenRouter) require both an environment variable AND Hermes auth registration. Even with a valid key, fallback won't work until both are set.  
548	
549	#### 7. Review Logs for Specific Errors  
550	Check the error logs for detailed failure information:  
551	```bash  
552	grep -i "together\|401" ~/.hermes/logs/errors.log | tail -20  
553	```  
554	Look for patterns in the failures.  
555	
556	#### 8. Test with Minimal Query  
557	Use a simple test query to avoid complexity:  
558	```bash  
559	hermes chat -q "Hello" --provider together --model meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo  
560	```  
561	
562	#### 9. Verify Model Availability  
563	Ensure the model name is correct for the provider:  
564	```bash  
565	# For Together AI  
566	curl -s https://api.together.xyz/v1/models | python3 -c "import json, sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print([m['id'] for m in d['data']])"  
567	```  
568	
569	#### 10. Restart Gateway After Changes  
570	Any configuration changes require a gateway restart:  
571	```bash  
572	hermes gateway restart  
573	```  
574	
575	#### Real-World Example: Together AI Fallback Failure  
576	**Symptoms:**  
577	- Explicit `--provider together` works  
578	- Fallback configuration returns 401 errors  
579	- Error shows `Endpoint: https://api.together.xyz/v1/` with trailing slash  
580	
581	**Diagnosis Steps:**  
582	1. Verified API key validity with curl  
583	2. Compared explicit vs fallback configurations  
584	3. Identified potential URL construction issue  
585	4. Tried both `provider: custom:together` and `provider: together`  
586	5. Removed trailing slash from base_url  
587	6. Switched to credential reference instead of api_key  
588	
589	**Resolution:** The exact fix depends on the specific issue, but this systematic approach will identify the root cause.

592	- **401 Unauthorized**: Invalid API key, missing auth registration, or malformed URL  
593	- **404 Not Found**: Incorrect base_url or endpoint path  
594	- **Provider missing from `hermes fallback`**: Credentials not set or invalid  
595	- **Fallback not triggering**: Primary provider not failing as expected

602	## Security & Privacy Toggles  
603	
604	Common "why is Hermes doing X to my output / tool calls / commands?" toggles — and the exact commands to change them. Most of these need a fresh session (`/reset` in chat, or start a new `hermes` invocation) because they're read once at startup.  
605	
606	### Secret redaction in tool output  
607	Secret redaction is **off by default** — tool output (terminal stdout, `read_file`, web content, subagent summaries, etc.) passes through unmodified. If the user wants Hermes to auto-mask strings that look like API keys, tokens, and secrets before they enter the conversation context and logs:  
608	```bash  
609	hermes config set security.redact_secrets true       # enable globally  
610	```  
611	**Restart required.** `security.redact_secrets` is snapshotted at import time — toggling it mid-session (e.g. via `export HERMES_REDACT_SECRETS=true` from a tool call) will NOT take effect for the running process. Tell the user to run `hermes config set security.redact_secrets true` in a terminal, then start a new session. This is deliberate — it prevents an LLM from flipping the toggle on itself mid-task.  
612	
613	Disable again with:  
614	```bash  
615	hermes config set security.redact_secrets false  
616	```  
617	
618	### PII redaction in gateway messages  
619	Separate from secret redaction. When enabled, the gateway hashes user IDs and strips phone numbers from the session context before it reaches the model:  
620	```bash  
621	hermes config set privacy.redact_pii true    # enable  
622	hermes config set privacy.redact_pii false   # disable (default)  
623	```  
624	
625	### Command approval prompts  
626	By default (`approvals.mode: manual`), Hermes prompts the user before running shell commands flagged as destructive (`rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, etc.). The modes are:  
627	- `manual` — always prompt (default)  
628	- `smart` — use an auxiliary LLM to auto-approve low-risk commands, prompt on high-risk  
629	- `off` — skip all approval prompts (equivalent to `--yolo`)  
630	
631	```bash  
632	hermes config set approvals.mode smart       # recommended middle ground  
633	hermes config set approvals.mode off         # bypass everything (not recommended)  
634	```  
635	Per-invocation bypass without changing config:  
636	- `hermes --yolo …`  
637	- `export HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1`  
638	
639	Note: YOLO / `approvals.mode: off` does NOT turn off secret redaction. They are independent.

642	Some shell-hook integrations require explicit allowlisting before they fire. Managed via `~/.hermes/shell-hooks-allowlist.json` — prompted interactively the first time a hook wants to run.

645	To keep the model away from network or media tools entirely, open `hermes tools` and toggle per-platform. Takes effect on next session (`/reset`). See the Tools & Skills section above.

683	## Spawning Additional Hermes Instances  
684	
685	Run additional Hermes processes as fully independent subprocesses — separate sessions, tools, and environments.  
686	
687	### When to Use This Vs delegate_task  
688	
689	| | `delegate_task` | Spawning `hermes` process |  
690	|-|-----------------|--------------------------|  
691	| Isolation | Separate conversation, shared process | Fully independent process |  
692	| Duration | Minutes (bounded by parent loop) | Hours/days |  
693	| Tool access | Subset of parent's tools | Full tool access |  
694	| Interactive | No | Yes (PTY mode) |  
695	| Use case | Quick parallel subtasks | Long autonomous missions |  
696	
697	### One-Shot Mode  
698	
699	```  
700	terminal(command="hermes chat -q 'Research GRPO papers and write summary to ~/research/grpo.md'", timeout=300)  
701	
702	# Background for long tasks:  
703	terminal(command="hermes chat -q 'Set up CI/CD for ~/myapp'", background=true)  
704	```  
705	
706	### Interactive PTY Mode (via tmux)  
707	
708	Hermes uses prompt_toolkit, which requires a real terminal. Use tmux for interactive spawning:  
709	
710	```  
711	# Start  
712	terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s agent1 -x 120 -y 40 'hermes'", timeout=10)  
713	
714	# Wait for startup, then send a message  
715	terminal(command="sleep 8 && tmux send-keys -t agent1 'Build a FastAPI auth service' Enter", timeout=15)  
716	
717	# Read output  
718	terminal(command="sleep 20 && tmux capture-pane -t agent1 -p", timeout=5)  
719	
720	# Send follow-up  
721	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t agent1 'Add rate limiting middleware' Enter", timeout=5)  
722	
723	# Exit  
724	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t agent1 '/exit' Enter && sleep 2 && tmux kill-session -t agent1", timeout=10)  
725	```  
726	
727	### Multi-Agent Coordination  
728	
729	```  
730	# Agent A: backend  
731	terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s backend -x 120 -y 40 'hermes -w'", timeout=10)  
732	terminal(command="sleep 8 && tmux send-keys -t backend 'Build REST API for user management' Enter", timeout=15)  
733	
734	# Agent B: frontend  
735	terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s frontend -x 120 -y 40 'hermes -w'", timeout=10)  
736	terminal(command="sleep 8 && tmux send-keys -t frontend 'Build React dashboard for user management' Enter", timeout=15)  
737	
738	# Check progress, relay context between them  
739	terminal(command="tmux capture-pane -t backend -p | tail -30", timeout=5)  
740	terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t frontend 'Here is the API schema from the backend agent: ...' Enter", timeout=5)  
741	```  
742	
743	### Session Resume  
744	
745	```  
746	# Resume most recent session  
747	terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s resumed 'hermes --continue'", timeout=10)  
748	
749	# Resume specific session  
750	terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s resumed 'hermes --resume 20260225_143052_a1b2c3'", timeout=10)  
751	```

753	### Tips  
754	
755	- **Prefer `delegate_task` for quick subtasks** — less overhead than spawning a full process  
756	- **Use `-w` (worktree mode)** when spawning agents that edit code — prevents git conflicts  
757	- **Set timeouts** for one-shot mode — complex tasks can take 5-10 minutes  
758	- **Use `hermes chat -q` for fire-and-forget** — no PTY needed  
759	- **Use tmux for interactive sessions** — raw PTY mode has `\r` vs `\n` issues with prompt_toolkit  
760	- **For scheduled tasks**, use the `cronjob` tool instead of spawning — handles delivery and retry

763	
764	For fleet-level agent lifecycle management — defining agents with IDENTITY.md, SOUL.md, HEARTBEAT.md, registering as shadow/observe-only, creating thin data-loading wrappers, and staging deployment via dry-run → live memory test → OS crontab activation with rollback guardrails — see the **shadow-agent-activation** skill.

809	   - `hermes crons` → `hermes cron ...` (singular command group)

811	   - `hermes pair` → `hermes pairing ...` (subcommands: `list`, `approve`, `revoke`, `clear-pending`)

898	### Platform-specific issues  
899	- **Discord bot silent**: Must enable **Message Content Intent** in Bot → Privileged Gateway Intents.  
900	- **Slack bot only works in DMs**: Must subscribe to `message.channels` event. Without it, the bot ignores public channels.  
901	- **Windows HTTP 400 "No models provided"**: Config file encoding issue (BOM). Ensure `config.yaml` is saved as UTF-8 without BOM.  
902	- **Telegram: token in .env but bot never connects** — `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` in `.env` is not enough on its own. The gateway also needs Telegram declared as an active platform in `config.yaml` under `platforms:`. If `platforms: {}`, Telegram is not wired in. Fix: run `hermes gateway setup`, select Telegram, let the wizard write the platform entry. Then `hermes gateway` will log `✓ telegram connected`.  
903	- **Telegram: TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS set to bot token prefix** — the numeric prefix of the bot token (e.g. `8663362298` from `8663362298:AAE...`) looks like a user ID but is the *bot's* ID, not yours. Get your personal user ID by messaging @userinfobot on Telegram. Using the bot ID here means the bot only accepts messages from itself and will never respond to you.  
904	- **Telegram: bot works in DMs but silent in groups** — privacy mode is on by default. Either disable it via @BotFather → /mybots → Bot Settings → Group Privacy → Turn off (then remove and re-add the bot to the group), or promote the bot to group admin.  
905	- **Telegram: voice replies land as audio file, not voice bubble** — edge-tts and other mp3-only providers need ffmpeg to convert to Opus. Install with `sudo apt install ffmpeg`. Without it, audio still sends but as a rectangular player, not a round voice bubble. See also: `references/hermes-tts-provider-codec-contracts.md` in `github-code-review`.  
906

908	If `auxiliary` tasks (vision, compression, session_search) fail silently, the `auto` provider can't find a backend. Either set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, or explicitly configure each auxiliary task's provider:  
909	```bash  
910	hermes config set auxiliary.vision.provider <your_provider>  
911	hermes config set auxiliary.vision.model <model_name>

18	# Self-Improving Skill
19	
20	Structured learning capture with promotion and demotion rules for persistent improvement.
21	
22	## When to Use
23	
24	- User corrects you or points out mistakes
25	- You complete significant work and want to evaluate the outcome
26	- You notice something in your own output that could be better
27	- Knowledge should compound over time without manual maintenance
28	
29	## Memory Architecture
30	
31	### Town Environment (Primary)
32	
33	Use Town's native memory system with tiered importance:
34	
35	| Tier | Storage | Purpose |
36	|------|---------|---------|
37	| HOT (critical) | `add_memory()` global | Always-active patterns affecting all routines |
38	| WARM (routine-specific) | `add_memory(routine_slug=...)` | Per-routine learned behaviors |
39	| COLD (archived) | Delete from active; note in user profile if historically significant | Decayed patterns no longer needed |
40	
41	### Hermes Environment (Secondary)
42	
43	File-based storage in `.learnings/`:
44	
45	| Tier | File | Limit | Purpose |
46	|------|------|-------|---------|
47	| HOT | `memory.md` | <=100 lines | Always loaded, most critical patterns |
48	| WARM | `projects/{name}.md` | <=200 lines each | Per-project learnings |
49	| WARM | `domains/{name}.md` | <=200 lines each | Domain-specific patterns |
50	| COLD | `archive/` | Unlimited | Decayed patterns |
51	| LOG | `corrections.md` | Last 50 | Raw correction log |
52	
53	## Learning Signals
54	
55	### Log immediately
56	- **Corrections**: "No, that's not right...", "Actually, it should be...", "You're wrong about...", "I prefer X, not Y", "Stop doing X"
57	- **Preferences**: "I like when you...", "Always do X for me", "Never do Y"
58	
59	### Track and promote after 3x
60	- **Patterns**: Recurring mistakes, recurring successes, recurring workarounds
61	
62	### Ignore
63	- One-time instructions
64	- Context-specific guidance
65	- Hypotheticals
66	
67	## Self-Reflection Framework
68	
69	After completing significant work:
70	1. Did it meet expectations?
71	2. What could be better?
72	3. Is this a pattern?
73	
74	Log format:
75	```
76	CONTEXT: [task type]
77	REFLECTION: [what I noticed]
78	LESSON: [what to do differently]
79	```
80	
81	## Core Rules
82	
83	### Rule 1 - Learning
84	Log explicit corrections and self-identified improvements. Never infer from silence. Confirm patterns after 3 identical lessons.
85	
86	### Rule 2 - Tiered Storage
87	- **HOT**: Critical patterns, active preferences (Town: global memories; Hermes: memory.md)
88	- **WARM**: Per-routine or per-project (Town: routine-scoped memories; Hermes: projects/*.md)
89	- **COLD**: Archived, decayed (Town: deleted with note; Hermes: archive/)
90	
91	### Rule 3 - Promotion / Demotion
92	- 3x in 7 days -> promote to HOT
93	- Unused 30 days -> demote to WARM
94	- Unused 90 days -> archive or delete
95

48	### Pipeline Steps (in order)

53	4. Audit

91	### Yahoo Finance Rate Limiting / Market Data Staleness
92	
93	**Symptom cascade**: Yahoo Finance API returns 429 (Too Many Requests) for ALL tickers including AAPL, XBI, AMGN. This is NOT a delisting event â€” it's rate limiting at Yahoo's end.

95	**Failure signature in logs**:
96	```
97	Failed to get ticker 'XBI' reason: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
98	XBI: No timezone found, symbol may be delisted
99	429 Client Error: Too Many Requests for url: https://query2.finance.yahoo.com/...
100	```
101	
102	**Affected pipeline steps**:
103	- **Step 1 (Price refresh)**: yfinance returns empty for every ticker â†’ 0 rows appended. Pipeline continues (non-fatal).
104	- **`collect_market_data.py`**: Network test catches the 429 â†’ falls back to cached data. `--force-refresh` does NOT circumvent this â€” the network test gates before the force override.
105	- **Step 5 (Gates â€” market data staleness)**: `market_data.json` age exceeds 3-day limit â†’ **abort** (hard gate).

107	**Diagnosis**:
108	1. Check `production_data/market_data.json` last-modified date vs today
109	2. Test yfinance connectivity: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" "https://query2.finance.yahoo.com/v10/finance/quoteSummary/AAPL?modules=financialData&corsDomain=finance.yahoo.com"`
110	3. Status code 429 = rate limited. Status code 200 = issue may be in the yfinance library or local environment.

112	**Remediation options**:

1	---
2	name: hermes-agent-skill-authoring
3	description: "Author in-repo SKILL.md: frontmatter, validator, structure."
4	version: 1.0.0
5	author: Hermes Agent
6	license: MIT
7	platforms: [linux, macos, windows]
8	metadata:
9	  hermes:
10	    tags: [skills, authoring, hermes-agent, conventions, skill-md]
11	    related_skills: [writing-plans, requesting-code-review]
12	---
13	
14	# Authoring Hermes-Agent Skills (in-repo)
15	
16	## Overview
17	
18	There are two places a SKILL.md can live:
19	
20	1. **User-local:** `~/.hermes/skills/<maybe-category>/<name>/SKILL.md` — personal, not shared. Created via `skill_manage(action='create')`.
21	2. **In-repo (this skill is about this case):** `/home/bb/hermes-agent/skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md` — committed, shipped with the package. Use `write_file` + `git add`. `skill_manage(action='create')` does NOT target this tree.
22	
23	## When to Use
24	
25	- User asks you to add a skill "in this branch / repo / commit"
26	- You're committing a reusable workflow that should ship with hermes-agent
27	- You're editing an existing skill under `/home/bb/hermes-agent/skills/` (use `patch` for small edits, `write_file` for rewrites; `skill_manage` still works for patch on in-repo skills, but not for `create`)
28	
29	## Required Frontmatter
30	
31	Source of truth: `tools/skill_manager_tool.py::_validate_frontmatter`. Hard requirements:
32	
33	- Starts with `---` as the first bytes (no leading blank line).
34	- Closes with `\n---\n` before the body.
35	- Parses as a YAML mapping.
36	- `name` field present.
37	- `description` field present, ≤ **1024 chars** (`MAX_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH`).
38	- Non-empty body after the closing `---`.
39	
40	Peer-matched shape used by every skill under `skills/software-development/`:
41	
42	```yaml
43	---
44	name: my-skill-name               # lowercase, hyphens, ≤64 chars (MAX_NAME_LENGTH)
45	description: Use when <trigger>. <one-line behavior>.
46	version: 1.0.0
47	author: Hermes Agent
48	license: MIT
49	metadata:
50	  hermes:
51	    tags: [short, descriptive, tags]
52	    related_skills: [other-skill, another-skill]
53	---
54	```
55	
56	`version` / `author` / `license` / `metadata` are NOT enforced by the validator, but every peer has them — omit and your skill sticks out.
57	
58	## Size Limits
59	
60	- Description: ≤ 1024 chars (enforced).
61	- Full SKILL.md: ≤ 100,000 chars (enforced as `MAX_SKILL_CONTENT_CHARS`, ~36k tokens).
62	- Peer skills in `software-development/` sit at **8-14k chars**. Aim for that range. If you're pushing past 20k, split into `references/*.md` and reference them from SKILL.md.
63	
64	## Peer-Matched Structure
65	
66	Every in-repo skill follows roughly:
67	
68	```
69	# <Title>
70	
71	## Overview
72	One or two paragraphs: what and why.
73	
74	## When to Use
75	- Bulleted triggers
76	- "Don't use for:" counter-triggers
77	
78	## <Topic sections specific to the skill>
79	- Quick-reference tables are common
80	- Code blocks with exact commands
81	- Hermes-specific recipes (tests via scripts/run_tests.sh, ui-tui paths, etc.)
82	
83	## Common Pitfalls
84	Numbered list of mistakes and their fixes.
85	
86	## Verification Checklist
87	- [ ] Checkbox list of post-action verifications
88	
89	## One-Shot Recipes (optional)
90	Named scenarios → concrete command sequences.
91	```
92	
93	Not every section is mandatory, but `Overview` + `When to Use` + actionable body + pitfalls are the minimum for the skill to feel like a peer.
94	
95	## Directory Placement
96	
97	```
98	skills/<category>/<skill-name>/SKILL.md
99	```
100	
101	Categories currently in repo (confirm with `ls skills/`): `autonomous-ai-agents`, `creative`, `data-science`, `devops`, `dogfood`, `email`, `gaming`, `github`, `leisure`, `mcp`, `media`, `mlops/*`, `note-taking`, `productivity`, `red-teaming`, `research`, `smart-home`, `social-media`, `software-development`.
102	
103	Pick the closest existing category. Don't invent new top-level categories casually.
104	
105	## Workflow
106	
107	1. **Survey peers** in the target category:
108	   ```
109	   ls skills/<category>/
110	   ```
111	   Read 2-3 peer SKILL.md files to match tone and structure.
112	2. **Check validator constraints** in `tools/skill_manager_tool.py` if unsure.
113	3. **Draft** with `write_file` to `skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md`.
114	4. **Validate locally**:
115	   ```python
116	   import yaml, re, pathlib
117	   content = pathlib.Path("skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md").read_text()
118	   assert content.startswith("---")
119	   m = re.search(r'\n---\s*\n', content[3:])
120	   fm = yaml.safe_load(content[3:m.start()+3])
121	   assert "name" in fm and "description" in fm
122	   assert len(fm["description"]) <= 1024
123	   assert len(content) <= 100_000
124	   ```
125	5. **Git add + commit** on the active branch.
126	6. **Note:** the CURRENT session's skill loader is cached — `skill_view` / `skills_list` will not see the new skill until a new session. This is expected, not a bug.
127	
128	## Cross-Referencing Other Skills
129	
130	`metadata.hermes.related_skills` unions both trees (`skills/` in-repo and `~/.hermes/skills/`) at load time. You CAN reference a user-local skill from an in-repo skill, but it won't resolve for other users who clone the repo fresh. Prefer referencing only in-repo skills from in-repo skills. If a frequently-referenced skill lives only in `~/.hermes/skills/`, consider promoting it to the repo.
131	
132	## Editing Existing In-Repo Skills
133	
134	- **Small fix (typo, added pitfall, tightened trigger):** `skill_manage(action='patch', name=..., old_string=..., new_string=...)` works fine on in-repo skills.
135	- **Major rewrite:** `write_file` the whole SKILL.md. `skill_manage(action='edit')` also works but requires supplying the full new content.
136	- **Adding supporting files:** `write_file` to `skills/<category>/<name>/references/<file>.md`, `templates/<file>`, or `scripts/<file>`. `skill_manage(action='write_file')` also works and enforces the references/templates/scripts/assets subdir allowlist.
137	- **Always commit** the edit — in-repo skills are source, not runtime state.
138	
139	## Common Pitfalls
140	
141	1. **Using `skill_manage(action='create')` for an in-repo skill.** It writes to `~/.hermes/skills/`, not the repo tree. Use `write_file` for in-repo creation.
142	
143	2. **Leading whitespace before `---`.** The validator checks `content.startswith("---")`; any leading blank line or BOM fails validation.
144	
145	3. **Description too generic.** Peer descriptions start with "Use when ..." and describe the *trigger class*, not the one task. "Use when debugging X" > "Debug X".
146	
147	4. **Forgetting the author/license/metadata block.** Not validator-enforced, but every peer has it; omitting makes the skill look half-finished.
148	
149	5. **Writing a skill that duplicates a peer.** Before creating, `ls skills/<category>/` and open 2-3 peers. Prefer extending an existing skill to creating a narrow sibling.
150	
151	6. **Expecting the current session to see the new skill.** It won't. The skill loader is initialized at session start. Verify in a fresh session or via `skill_view` using the exact path.
152	
153	7. **Linking to skills that don't exist in-repo.** `related_skills: [some-user-local-skill]` works for you but breaks for other clones. Prefer only in-repo links.
154	
155	## Verification Checklist
156	
157	- [ ] File is at `skills/<category>/<name>/SKILL.md` (not in `~/.hermes/skills/`)
158	- [ ] Frontmatter starts at byte 0 with `---`, closes with `\n---\n`
159	- [ ] `name`, `description`, `version`, `author`, `license`, `metadata.hermes.{tags, related_skills}` all present
160	- [ ] Name ≤ 64 chars, lowercase + hyphens
161	- [ ] Description ≤ 1024 chars and starts with "Use when ..."
162	- [ ] Total file ≤ 100,000 chars (aim for 8-15k)
163	- [ ] Structure: `# Title` → `## Overview` → `## When to Use` → body → `## Common Pitfalls` → `## Verification Checklist`
164	- [ ] `related_skills` references resolve in-repo (or are explicitly OK to be user-local)
165	- [ ] `git add skills/<category>/<name>/ && git commit` completed on the intended branch

Here is a comprehensive report on how Hermes skills work from the inside.

---

## SKILL.md Format: Canonical Structure

### Required Frontmatter (enforced by validator in `tools/skill_manager_tool.py`)

The validator (`_validate_frontmatter`) enforces exactly three hard constraints:
1. File must start at byte 0 with `---` (no leading whitespace or BOM)
2. Frontmatter must close with `\n---\n`
3. `name` field must be present (max 64 chars, lowercase + hyphens)
4. `description` field must be present (max 1024 chars)
5. Non-empty body must follow the closing `---`
6. Total file size must be under 100,000 chars (~36k tokens)

Everything beyond `name` and `description` is conventional, not enforced.

### Full Conventional Frontmatter Shape

Every peer skill under `software-development/` uses this full shape:

```yaml
---
name: skill-name                          # lowercase, hyphens, ≤64 chars
description: "Use when <trigger>. ..."    # ≤1024 chars, starts "Use when..."
version: 1.0.0
author: Hermes Agent
license: MIT
platforms: [linux, macos, windows]        # omit = all platforms
metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [tag1, tag2, tag3]
    related_skills: [other-skill]
    fallback_for_toolsets: [toolset-name]  # optional conditional activation
    requires_toolsets: [toolset-name]      # optional conditional activation
    fallback_for_tools: [tool-name]        # optional
    requires_tools: [tool-name]            # optional
    config:                                # optional config var declarations
      - key: wiki.path
        description: Path to the wiki
        default: "~/wiki"
        prompt: Wiki directory path
---
```

### The `triggers` field (user-local skills only)

The `triggers` field appears in some user-local skills (e.g., `autonomous-ai-agents/self-improving` and `biotech-screener/dossier-generation`). The hermes-agent source code does **not** process `triggers` as a machine-readable dispatch field. It is not referenced anywhere in `skill_utils.py`, `skill_commands.py`, or the validator. It functions as human-readable documentation — the same information could go in a "When to Use" section of the body. Its presence in user-local skills appears to be a personal convention for Darren's skills, not a system-enforced field.

### The `tags` field (user-local variants)

Some user-local skills (e.g., `biotech-screener/screener-ops`) use `tags:` at the top level of frontmatter rather than nested under `metadata.hermes.tags`. Again, this is not processed by the validator or loader — it is decorative.

---

## The Two SKILL.md Variants Observed

### Variant 1: Hub/in-repo skills (canonical)

Used by skills shipped with hermes-agent under `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/skills/`. Full frontmatter with `name`, `description`, `version`, `author`, `license`, `platforms`, `metadata.hermes.{tags, related_skills}`. Body structured as: `# Title` → `## Overview` → `## When to Use` → topic sections → `## Common Pitfalls` → `## Verification Checklist`.

Example: `/home/arrenchulz/.hermes/hermes-agent/skills/software-development/hermes-agent-skill-authoring/SKILL.md`

### Variant 2: User-local / operator skills

Used under `~/.hermes/skills/`. Lighter frontmatter. Some use only `name` + `description` (memory-steward, ai-landscape-monitoring). Some add `triggers:` lists and `tags:` at the top level (self-improving, dossier-generation, screener-ops). The `hermes-link` hub skill from `~/.hermeslink/` uses only `name` + `description` — the minimal valid shape.

The key structural difference from in-repo skills: user-local skills often carry much more operational content, function more like reference manuals or runbooks than instruction guides, and use `triggers:` as a human-readable signal for when the skill applies.

---

## How a Skill Gets Invoked

There are three invocation paths, all defined in `/home/arrenchulz/.hermes/hermes-agent/agent/skill_commands.py`:

### 1. Slash command in-session: `/skill-name`
The skill name maps directly to a slash command. Typing `/screener-ops` or `/self-improving` in a Hermes chat session invokes `build_skill_invocation_prompt()`, which loads the SKILL.md content and injects it into the conversation as:

```
[IMPORTANT: The user has invoked the "skill-name" skill, indicating they want you to follow its instructions. The full skill content is loaded below.]
```

The skill body is then appended in full. The model reads and follows it as active instructions.

### 2. Session preload: `hermes -s skill-name` or `hermes --skills skill-name`
Invokes `build_preloaded_skills_prompt()`. The injected activation note differs:

```
[IMPORTANT: The user launched this CLI session with the "skill-name" skill preloaded. Treat its instructions as active guidance for the duration of this session unless the user overrides them.]
```

### 3. In-session slash command: `/skill skill-name`
Also resolves via `build_skill_invocation_prompt()`. Same activation note as path 1.

Skills are NOT automatically dispatched based on natural language matching. There is no trigger-matching engine that routes messages to skills based on the `triggers:` field. Invocation is always explicit (slash command, `--skills` flag, or the `/skill` command).

---

### Curator backup manifests (`~/.hermes/skills/.curator_backups/*/manifest.json`)

These are not skill manifests — they are backup metadata. Structure:

```json
{
```
